```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      warning = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.8,
                      fig.align = "center")
```

A list of meta-DEGs is the starting point for biology, not the end. Module 9
turns a meta-signature into testable hypotheses using public prior
knowledge. It answers four questions:

1. **Transcription factors.** Which regulators explain the signature?
2. **Cell composition.** Is the signature caused by shifts in cell types?
3. **Co-expression.** Which gene programs are shared by all cohorts?
4. **Drug reversal.** Which compounds reverse the disease state?

The demo uses a **pan-cancer tumour vs adjacent-normal** meta-analysis of
three GEO cohorts. The question is which tumour programs are shared by
colorectal (GSE130688), pancreatic (GSE136569) and renal clear-cell
(GSE171485) carcinomas. All counts are NCBI GEO-generated raw counts. The
shipped file contains real inputs:

- the **genome-wide** random-effects meta-analysis (29,560 genes);
- the three cohorts, restricted to cell-type markers and the 1,500 most
  variable genes, with their true library sizes;
- the CollecTRI TF-target network (Mueller-Dott et al. 2023);
- MCP-counter markers (Becht et al. 2016);
- 200 LINCS L1000 drug signatures (Subramanian et al. 2017).

Because the three tumour types differ, interpret the pooled effects as
"shared across these carcinomas", not as one disease. For a single-disease
analysis, see `vignette("case_study")`.

```{r load}
library(metaXpress)
ds <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "case_study_downstream.rds",
                          package = "metaXpress"))
ds$meta_result
nrow(ds$collectri)     # TF-target interactions
length(ds$lincs)       # drug signatures in the demo subset
```

## 1. Transcription factor activity

Which upstream regulators explain the shared tumour program? `mx_tf_activity()` regresses the signed meta z-score of every gene on each TF's target weights (decoupleR's ULM method):

```{r tf-activity, fig.height=6}
tf <- mx_tf_activity(ds$meta_result, ds$collectri, id_col = "symbol",
                     min_size = 10)
head(tf, 10)
mx_downstream_plot(tf, top = 20)
```

These results come from the **genome-wide** meta-signature, so they are identical to the full case study. Of 548 TFs with at least 10 measured targets, 65 are significant (FDR < 0.05):
* the **E2F family** (E2F1–E2F4) drives cell-cycle genes, a proliferation program shared by all three carcinomas;
* **NF-κB** (RELA, REL, RELB) and **AP-1** (JUN) indicate a common inflammatory-signalling component;
* SNAI2, CEBPA and HDAC4 are the significantly repressed regulators.

## 2. Cell-type composition

Could the signal be caused by tumours simply containing more immune or stromal cells? `mx_cell_composition()` scores each sample for each cell type, computes Hedges' g per cohort and pools them:

```{r composition, fig.height=4}
comp <- mx_cell_composition(ds$studies, ds$markers)
comp[, c("cell_type", "meta_g", "padj", "i_squared",
         grep("^g_", names(comp), value = TRUE))]
mx_downstream_plot(comp)
```

No cell population changes significantly after FDR correction. The per-cohort columns show why the pooled effects are all positive: the colorectal cohort has large effects (g ≈ 1.0–1.6), while pancreatic and renal are near zero. A consistent immune or stromal shift therefore does **not** explain the shared meta-DEGs, which supports them as tumour-intrinsic. CD8 T cells are dropped because only one of their markers was measured.

## 3. Consensus co-expression modules

`mx_coexpression_modules()` finds gene programs whose co-expression holds in **every** cohort (minimum correlation across studies), then tests each module's eigengene between tumour and normal:

```{r coexpression, fig.height=4}
net <- mx_coexpression_modules(ds$studies, n_genes = 1500, cut_height = 0.3,
                               min_module_size = 20,
                               meta_result = ds$meta_result)
ms <- net$module_stats
# Hub genes are Entrez IDs; show symbols stored in rowData
sym <- setNames(SummarizedExperiment::rowData(ds$studies[[1]])$symbol,
                rownames(ds$studies[[1]]))
ms$hub_genes <- vapply(strsplit(ms$hub_genes, ", "),
                       function(g) paste(sym[g], collapse = ", "), character(1))
ms[, c("module", "n_genes", "meta_g", "padj", "pct_meta_up", "hub_genes")]
mx_downstream_plot(net)
```

The leading module (M2) has **MST1R** as its top hub, alongside TSPAN1, B3GNT3 and ITGB4. MST1R is among the top gene-level meta-DEGs, and here it emerges independently as the centre of an epithelial program co-expressed in all three cohorts; over a third of M2's genes are significant meta-DEGs. In this reduced 1,500-gene demo M2 does not reach FDR significance (FDR = 0.14). In the full case study (3,000 genes) the same MST1R/CDCP1 module is significant (FDR = 0.043). The other modules capture tissue-of-origin programs (immunoglobulin, islet/neuroendocrine, smooth muscle, ribosomal RNA) rather than tumour biology.

## 4. Drug signature reversal

Which compounds push expression in the opposite direction to the tumour state? `mx_drug_connectivity()` scores each drug's up/down gene sets against the meta-ranking (negative = reverses the disease):

```{r drugs, fig.height=6}
drugs <- mx_drug_connectivity(ds$meta_result, ds$lincs, id_col = "symbol")
head(drugs, 10)
mx_downstream_plot(drugs, top = 20)
```

The ranking matches the full 5,425-compound analysis. **Three of the top five compounds (SD-208, GW-788388, LY-2109761) inhibit the TGF-β type I receptor (ALK5).** The other top hits target CDKs (R-547), MEK (TAK-733), p300/CBP (C646) and MDM2 (SAR405838), which fits the E2F-driven proliferation found in Section 1.

> **Caveats.** This demo ships only 200 of the 5,425 LINCS signatures, chosen from the full ranking, so the adjusted p-values here are not meaningful. Even in the full analysis the p-values assume independent genes and are anti-conservative, so use the score for ranking only. LINCS signatures come from cancer cell lines, so these hits are hypotheses for experimental follow-up. The full analysis is reproduced by `scripts/run_case_study_applications.R` in the package source repository.
